h1: Who is the best SEO agency? The question behind the question
metaTitle: Who Is the Best SEO Agency? Ask This Instead
metaDescription: There is no best SEO agency, only the best fit. How award lists and agency directories are actually funded, and the four questions worth asking instead.
answer: There is no best SEO agency, and no body that awards the title. Most lists claiming to rank one are funded by the agencies on them — through paid directory placement, awards with entry fees, or affiliate posts. The useful question is narrower: which agency fits your market, your budget and your constraints?
takeaways: No governing body ranks SEO agencies. Every list you'll find is a **commercial product**, and you can usually confirm that in under a minute.
A global ranking is close to useless locally. Link sources, SERP features and language are all national.
Fit beats reputation: demand shape, the actual bottleneck, what you can supply, and what happens if it fails.
Client **tenure** is the most under-used check in agency selection. Three clients held past 18 months tells you more than thirty logos.

sections.h2: Why nobody can hold the title
body: There's no exam, no register and no shared scoreboard. SEO has no equivalent of a bar council or a chartered body, so "best" is a claim anyone can make and nobody can adjudicate.

Even if someone tried, the metric would collapse immediately. An agency that's brilliant at recovering a 40,000-URL ecommerce catalogue after a botched migration may be genuinely bad at getting a three-location dental clinic into the map pack. Those are different disciplines wearing the same job title.

Scale breaks it further. The agencies with the biggest names usually have minimum retainers that exceed what a ₹15 lakh annual marketing budget can carry, and the ones that would take your budget don't get written about. "Best" and "available to you" rarely overlap.

callout.title: A better sentence to say out loud
callout.body: Swap "who's the best SEO agency" for "who has fixed this specific problem, in this market, for a business my size, in the last eighteen months". The second question has an answer. The first doesn't.

sections.h2: How 'top SEO agency' lists are actually funded
body: You don't have to take anyone's word on this, including ours. Every list has a business model, and the model is usually one click away in the footer. Here's what to look for.

table.caption: Three ways a 'top SEO agencies' list gets paid — and how to verify each one.
head: List type
How it's funded
The 60-second check
rows: Agencies pay for sponsored placement, premium profiles or access to leads. Free profiles sit underneath the paid ones.
Find the 'Advertise', 'For agencies' or 'Get listed' link in the footer and read the pricing page. Then check whether the top entries carry a 'sponsored' or 'featured' tag.
Entries carry a fee, frequently per category. More categories entered, more chances of winning something to put on the homepage.
Open the 'Enter now' page. Look for the entry fee, the category count and the judging panel. Ask whether judges were paid and whether finalists bought a table.
Written by a publisher selling placement, an affiliate earning commission, or one of the agencies on the list.
Check whether the outbound links are tagged sponsored or nofollow, whether the author has a real named byline, and whether the site sells anything to agencies.

callout.title: The reviews are real. The order isn't.
callout.body: Most directory reviews are collected from actual clients — that part is usually legitimate. What's sold is **position**: who appears above the fold, who gets the badge, who receives the lead. Read the reviews. Ignore the ranking.

sections.h2: Why a 'best in the world' ranking ignores your market
body: Search results are national, and so is almost everything that produces them. The links that move a UK site come from UK publishers, associations and universities. An agency with brilliant relationships at London mastheads has none in Mumbai, and vice versa.

Language compounds it. If a meaningful share of your buyers search in Hindi, Bengali, Tamil or Arabic — or in the Roman-script hybrid most Indians actually type — a globally famous agency will hand that work to a translation vendor and hope.

SERP shape differs too. What Google shows for a query in India is often not what it shows for the same query in the US: different pack sizes, different aggregators sitting above you, different competitors entirely. Strategy built on one country's SERP doesn't port. If you're shopping across borders, [Indian agency versus international agency](/compare/indian-seo-agency-vs-international-agency) is the more honest comparison.

sections.h2: The four fit questions that actually decide it
body: These four replace the ranking. Answer them yourself first, in writing, before you speak to anybody. Half the shortlist disqualifies itself the moment you do.
numbered: **What shape is my demand?** Map-pack local, national commercial, or multi-country and multi-language. These need three different agencies. An agency that lives in Google Business Profile optimisation is not the one to run a 12-market hreflang rollout.

**What's actually broken?** Not enough traffic, wrong traffic, or traffic that doesn't convert. If your problem is the third one, hiring a content shop buys you more of a thing that already isn't working. Get a diagnosis before you buy a treatment.

**What can I supply?** SEO fails on the client side more often than the agency side. Can you give them developer time, subject-matter interviews, and approvals inside a week? If approvals take a month, buy less content and more technical work.

**What happens if it doesn't work?** Ask it plainly and watch. Most answers are a variation of "we'd review the strategy", which means the invoice arrives regardless. Anything more specific — a clause, a baseline, a stop point — is a real answer.

body: A logo wall proves someone signed once. Tenure proves someone stayed. It's the single most informative check in agency selection and almost nobody runs it, because it takes ten minutes and it's slightly awkward to ask.
Ask for it directly: three clients they've held for eighteen months or more, and the reason the last three departures left. Then verify independently.
bullets: Pull their client page through the **Wayback Machine** at 12 and 24 months back. A logo wall that turns over completely every year is churn dressed as growth.
Check the **account lead's LinkedIn tenure**, not the founder's. If the person who'd run your account joined eleven weeks ago, they'll learn your category on your budget.
Look for **dates on case studies**. Undated usually means old. A 2019 result presented in 2026 predates several core updates and the whole AI Overviews shift.
Ask to speak to a client who **left**. Refusing is a legitimate answer — plenty of exits are under NDA — but how they refuse is informative.
Ask what they've **declined recently**. An agency that has never turned down a brief has no thesis about who they're good for.

callout.title: The pitch team problem
callout.body: The people who win the pitch are frequently not the people who do the work. Ask "will the people in this room run my account?" and get the names into the contract. It costs nothing and prevents the most common post-signature disappointment.

sections.h2: What to do with a shortlist you found online
body: Don't throw it away. A paid list is still a list of agencies that exist, employ people and answer email — that's a starting set, just not a ranking. Treat it as raw material and run this.
numbered: Strip the order. Alphabetise it so the paid position stops influencing you.
Cut anyone whose stated minimum is more than you'll spend, and anyone whose case studies are all in a different market or a different business model.
Send the same brief to three, with the same deadline. Different briefs make proposals impossible to compare, which is exactly why agencies prefer them.
Score the proposals on one line only: **what number will we measure, and what is it today?** If a proposal can't state your current baseline, they haven't looked at your data.
Run the tenure check on the two that survive.
Read the exit clause before the pricing. A twelve-month lock-in with a 90-day notice period is a nine-month bet on strangers.

faqs.a: Most of them, in one of three ways: sponsored placement on a directory, awards with per-category entry fees, or affiliate and placement deals on editorial listicles. You can check any list in under a minute — look for an 'advertise with us' page, a 'sponsored' tag on the top entries, or sponsored-tagged outbound links.

faqs.q: Which SEO agency is best for a small business in India?
faqs.a: Whichever one will actually staff your account rather than park it. Under roughly ₹40,000 a month, a strong specialist freelancer usually beats a cheap agency because you get senior hours instead of a junior plus a manager. Above that, an agency's range across technical, content and links starts to pay for itself.

faqs.q: Do awards mean an SEO agency is good?
faqs.a: They mean the agency entered, paid the fee and wrote a good submission — which correlates with marketing ability, not delivery. Awards judged by named practitioners on verifiable client outcomes carry some signal. Awards with fifty categories and a gala dinner carry almost none.

faqs.q: How do I verify an SEO agency's case studies?
faqs.a: Ask for the live URL of the page that ranked, then check it yourself: search the claimed keyword, look at the page in the Wayback Machine around the claimed dates, and see whether the client still credits them. Ask for a live Search Console screen share rather than a cropped screenshot.

faqs.q: Should I hire the agency that ranks first for 'best SEO agency'?
faqs.a: It proves they can rank a page in a low-competition, low-intent niche. That's a mild positive signal and nothing more — the query is dominated by directories and their own service page competes with almost nobody. Judge them on client outcomes in your market instead.
